review:
Michael Mann shoots Los Angeles the way other directors shoot the ocean — as something vast, indifferent, and faintly luminous at three in the morning. Every glass tower in this film is lit from within and empty. The city is the third lead, and it never says a word.

The famous coffee shop scene works because it refuses to be a duel. De Niro and Pacino sit across from each other and discover, with something close to disappointment, that they are the same man with different paperwork. Neither performance reaches for the moment. They underplay it into something closer to a confession, and the film never quite recovers its balance afterwards — which is the point.

What surprises on a rewatch is how much of the runtime is domestic. The heists are procedural and cold; the marriages are where the violence actually lands. Mann keeps cutting back to women waiting in kitchens, and the cumulative effect is that the downtown shootout feels less like a climax than an admission that none of these men know how to be anywhere else.

It is too long. It is also close to perfect, and the length is part of why.
